design_detail: Cross-sectional analysis of the Global Drug Survey 2014 (GDS), an anonymous, self-selected online survey that ran for five weeks from mid-November 2013 and was promoted through social media and media partners (Fairfax Media, MixMag, The Guardian). Lifetime, last-12-month and last-30-day nitrous oxide use were asked within a screen of 134 substances (74,864 respondents; prevalence shown for the whole sample and six countries). Respondents who had used nitrous oxide in the last 12 months (below, last-year respondents; n=4883) answered questions on method, sources, places, amount per session in 'hits' (one hit taken as one balloon, typically the contents of one cream charger), days of use in the last 30 days, use with other drugs, six adverse effects experienced in relation to nitrous oxide (in the last 12 months, earlier, or never), and worry about effects on mental and physical health. Descriptive and unweighted, with 95% intervals; Table 4 gives mean hits per session for those reporting each adverse effect. The PDF read is the online-first version (pages 1–7).
can_establish: What self-selected GDS 2014 respondents reported about nitrous oxide use (lifetime, last year and last month, by country) and, among those who had used it in the last 12 months, how they used it and how many reported each of six adverse effects and each level of worry.
cannot_establish: How common nitrous oxide use or its harms are in any general population (self-selected online sample); whether the reported numbness, accidents or other effects were caused by nitrous oxide rather than by other drugs taken with it (89% used it with other drugs), or were clinically real (single self-report items, no examination); whether larger amounts per session cause harm (the analysis offered as dose–response has no comparison with unaffected respondents and no adjustment); or anything about dependence, which was not measured.

sample.recruitment: Self-nominating online survey: GDS 2014 ran for five weeks at the end of 2013, launched in mid-November and promoted through social media and media partners including Fairfax Media, MixMag and The Guardian; almost 80,000 people from over 150 countries took part (PDF p. 2, Introduction, 6th paragraph; Methods › Design, 1st paragraph); 74,864 respondents are analysed (Table 1, PDF p. 3). The authors call the method purposive sampling (PDF p. 3, Sampling strategy). Ethics approval by the Joint South London and Maudsley and Institute of Psychiatry NHS Research Ethics Committee (PDF p. 3, Methods › Design, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated: no eligibility criteria, data-cleaning rules or exclusions are described, and the difference between almost 80,000 participants and 74,864 analysed is not explained. The adverse-effect and worry questions were put to all respondents who had used nitrous oxide in the last 12 months (PDF p. 3, Measures, 2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Last-year respondents (n=4883): mean age 24.3 (SD 6.7), median 22 (IQR 20–27). Last-year prevalence 7.2% among men (3555) and 4.9% among women (1190), 9.4% among clubbers (3710; clubbing at least once every three months, n=39,666) and 3.0% among non-clubbers (1009) (Table 2, PDF p. 4). The country, education and other characteristics of this subsample are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single survey). The six adverse-effect items were answered by between 4622 and 4653 of the 4883 last-year respondents (editors' sums of the Table 3 counts); these unprinted numbers are the denominators of the percentages in Table 3 and the abstract.
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected readers of the survey's media partners and social media, weighted towards people who use drugs and go clubbing; the authors acknowledge that this selection limits generalizability (PDF p. 3, Sampling strategy) and that the self-nominating sample may not represent people who use nitrous oxide (PDF p. 4, Limitations). For comparison, the paper cites a last-year prevalence of 2% among 16–59-year-olds in the 2012/13 Crime Survey for England and Wales (PDF p. 2), against 20.5% among this survey's UK respondents. By the editors' arithmetic from Table 1, about 1471 (30%) of the 4883 last-year respondents were from the UK and about 778 (16%) from Germany, so the adverse-effect shares lean towards those two countries. People with severe harm (hospital admission, disability, death) are unlikely to be among respondents.

exposure.measurement: Self-report online: lifetime, last-12-month and last-30-day use within a 134-substance screen; among last-year respondents, main method, route, sources, places, number of hits per session (one hit taken as one balloon, typically the contents of one cream charger), days used in the last 30 days and use with other drugs (PDF p. 3, Measures, 1st paragraph). Nothing was verified.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Recorded here only as measured use patterns. Last-year respondents: balloon 80.6% (3787), whipped-cream dispenser 15.9% (745), plastic bag 0.8% (39), gas bulb 0.8% (38), other 1.9% (90); inhaled by mouth 98.3% (4602); median 5 hits per session (IQR 3–10) (Table 2, PDF p. 4). Among respondents who had used it in the last 30 days, median 2 days of use in that period (IQR 1–3) in the whole sample (Table 1, PDF p. 3).
exposure.polysubstance: 89.2% (4354) of last-year respondents reported using nitrous oxide with other drugs (Table 2, PDF p. 4); which drugs is not reported, and the adverse-effect results are not adjusted for co-use. Table 3 gives the share using other drugs among those reporting each effect (for example 91.1% of those with an accident in the last 12 months against 88.6% of those who never had one).

comparison.controls: None for the adverse effects: Table 3 places respondents reporting each effect in the last 12 months, earlier, or never side by side, without statistical tests, and Table 4 gives mean hits per session only for those reporting each effect. Prevalence is compared across six countries.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Neurological symptoms, vitamin B12 status, diet, other health conditions and other drug use before or at the time were not measured; the persistent numbness item does not separate symptoms that began before nitrous oxide use.

outcomes.instruments: Study-specific questions. Adverse effects: "Have you ever experienced any of the following in relation to use of nitrous?" with fainting, accidental injury, nausea, confusion, hallucinations, and persistent numbness or tingling in arms and legs lasting days and weeks after using, each answered as in the last 12 months, earlier, or never (PDF p. 3, Measures, 2nd paragraph; Table 3, PDF pp. 4–5). Worry about the effect of use on mental and on physical health: no; yes, a little; yes, a lot (Table 5, PDF p. 6). A well-being mean score (54.9) is listed in Table 2 without naming the instrument.
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation or reliability data. The adverse effects are single self-report items attributed to nitrous oxide by the respondents; persistent numbness or tingling was not clinically confirmed, and the authors say further work is needed to confirm persistent neurological symptoms (abstract, PDF p. 1).
outcomes.operationalization: Harm = self-reported experience of each effect in relation to nitrous oxide use, in the last 12 months or earlier; heavier use = more hits per session; a dose–response relation is inferred from comparing mean hits per session across groups reporting different effects (Table 4, PDF p. 5).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive percentages with 95% intervals; no hypothesis tests are reported. Eight outcome items for last-year respondents (six adverse effects and two worry items).

analysis.effect_sizes: Prevalence with 95% CI (Table 1, PDF p. 3): whole sample (n=74,864) lifetime 18.8% (18.5–19.1), last 12 months 6.5% (6.3–6.7), last 30 days 2.2% (2.1–2.3); UK (n=7174) 38.6% (37.5–39.7), 20.5% (19.6–21.5) and 7.7% (7.1–8.3); Germany (n=22,232) 11.2% (10.8–11.6), 3.5% (3.3–3.7) and 0.9% (0.8–1.0). Adverse effects in the last 12 months among last-year respondents who answered (about 4620–4650): hallucinations 27.8% (1289), confusion 24.0% (1108), nausea 5.8% (267), fainting 4.4% (205), persistent numbness 4.3% (200), accidents 1.2% (56) (Table 3, PDF pp. 4–5). No intervals are given for these shares; for persistent numbness, 200 of 4633, the 95% interval is 3.8% to 4.9% (editors' calculation, Wilson), which reflects sampling error only, not selection. Mean hits per session (95% CI from a Poisson distribution) among those reporting each effect in the last 12 months: accidents 27.4 (26.0–28.8), fainting 21.1 (20.5–21.7), persistent numbness 15.1 (14.6–15.7), nausea 14.4 (13.9–14.8), hallucinations 12.8 (12.6–13.0) (Table 4, PDF p. 5).
analysis.covariates: None: all results are unweighted and unadjusted (PDF p. 3, Statistical analysis).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned (registries not searched).
analysis.selective_reporting: Six countries are shown (the text says seven) without saying why these; confusion is missing from Table 4, which gives no figures for respondents without each effect; no test supports the dose–response statement; dependence is discussed but no dependence measure is reported.
analysis.power: Not applicable to the descriptive aims; not reported.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In a self-selected online sample of 74,864 people (GDS 2014), 18.8% reported lifetime and 6.5% last-year nitrous oxide use, most among UK respondents (38.6% lifetime, 20.5% last year). Of about 4630 last-year respondents who answered, 27.8% reported hallucinations and 24.0% confusion related to nitrous oxide in the last 12 months, 4.3% persistent numbness or tingling lasting days or weeks, and 1.2% an accidental injury; counting earlier reports too, 5.9% ever reported persistent numbness and 3.2% an accident (editors' calculations from Table 3). Respondents reporting each effect reported more hits per session (accidents: median 15 against 5 among those who never had one), and 89% used nitrous oxide with other drugs. Most were not worried about effects on their health.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the analysis confirms that nitrous oxide is associated with hallucinations, confusion, persistent numbness and accidental injury, that the link between accidental injury and the most hits per session suggests a dose–response relationship, that most people use it infrequently without significant harm, and that a subpopulation may be using in a dependent pattern (abstract, PDF p. 1); the Conclusions add that the findings largely suggest that legislation to ban nitrous oxide is unnecessary (PDF p. 5). Gaps: (1) no comparison group or test supports the dose–response statement; the intervals in Table 4 assume Poisson variation, which the medians and interquartile ranges in Table 3 contradict; and amount per session is confounded with frequency of use, co-use and opportunities for accidents. (2) Harm by frequency of use is described (Table 3 gives median days of use for each effect group) but not tested, so the statement about infrequent use is untested. (3) Dependence was not measured. (4) The policy conclusion goes beyond survey data on self-reported effects. The abstract and Conclusions also place use mainly at festivals and clubs, while Table 2 shows house parties (72.2%) and the respondent's own home (51.4%) as common as or more common than festivals (53.3%) and clubs (31.8%). A headline version (4% of people who use nitrous oxide get nerve damage) would overstate: these are self-reported, unconfirmed symptoms in the last 12 months among self-selected last-year respondents.

timeline.event: Erowid online survey of 11,551 respondents: 65% had ever used nitrous oxide; most had used it fewer than ten times, 14% more than 100 times, and 17% reported more than 25 cartridges in an average session; as cited by this paper (PDF p. 2, Introduction, 4th paragraph); not read.
Crime Survey for England and Wales 2012/13: last-year prevalence 2% at ages 16–59 and 6% at ages 16–24; as cited by this paper (PDF p. 2, Introduction, 5th paragraph); not read.
This survey (GDS 2014, fielded at the end of 2013).
Oussalah et al., systematic review of published case reports, cites this survey's 4.3% persistent numbness and 1.2% accidental injury (project card sc_oussalah_2019).

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: only this survey was read for this card. Against the companion card sc_oussalah_2019, which pools 100 published cases and cannot say how often harm occurs, this survey supplies a denominator, but a self-selected one: 200 of about 4630 last-year respondents (4.3%) reported persistent numbness or tingling in the last 12 months and 274 (5.9%) ever, self-reported and clinically unconfirmed. Oussalah et al. cite the 4.3% and 1.2% as shares of people who had used nitrous oxide; they are last-12-month reports among people who had used it in the last year and answered each item. The survey's own data show only a small difference in typical amount between respondents with and without persistent numbness (median hits per session 6 against 5), so it does not establish at what exposure nerve symptoms occur.

funding.funder: The authors received no financial support for the research, authorship and/or publication of the article (PDF p. 6, Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declared no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship and/or publication of the article (PDF p. 6, Declaration of Conflicting Interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Addiction Clinical Academic Group, South London and Maudsley NHS Trust; Institute for Social Science Research and ARC Centre of Excellence for Children and Families over the Life Course, University of Queensland; Global Drug Survey, London; TICTAC Communications Ltd, St George's, University of London (PDF p. 1). Four of the six authors list Global Drug Survey, which runs the survey and produced the harm-reduction tips in Figure 2. Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A survey of a probability sample (or a cohort) of people who use nitrous oxide that measures amount, frequency and duration of use and co-use, with clinically confirmed neurological outcomes (examination, vitamin B12 and related markers, nerve conduction) in those reporting symptoms and in a comparison group, analysed with adjustment, to estimate how often persistent neurological harm occurs and how it varies with exposure.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: No frame: an open online survey promoted through social media and media partners.

domains.domain: 2. Participants sampled appropriately
domains.note: Self-nominating volunteers; the authors call it purposive sampling and acknowledge selection bias.

domains.domain: 3. Adequate sample size
domains.note: 74,864 respondents and 4883 last-year respondents give precise shares for this sample (for example 4.3%, 95% interval 3.8–4.9%, editors' calculation).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Age, sex, clubbing, methods, sources and places are described for last-year respondents (Table 2), but not their countries, education or the drugs used with nitrous oxide; the well-being instrument is unnamed.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: The adverse-effect items were answered by about 95% of last-year respondents (editors' calculation), with denominators unprinted; the gap between almost 80,000 participants and 74,864 analysed is unexplained.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Single unvalidated self-report items, attributed to nitrous oxide by respondents; persistent numbness or tingling not clinically confirmed; 89% co-use.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: The same online questions for all last-year respondents; no reliability data; amount per session approximated by counting balloons.

domains.domain: 8. Appropriate statistical analysis
domains.note: Intervals computed as if from a random sample; Poisson intervals for strongly skewed counts in Table 4; no comparison group or test for the dose–response statement; no adjustment.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed
domains.note: Open web survey with no denominator of people reached; no response rate can be computed and no weighting was applied.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist (editors' summary: high risk of bias) because the encyclopedia will use the survey's prevalence figures and shares of respondents reporting each effect. The shares are precise for this sample but describe self-selected GDS respondents, weighted towards UK and German respondents and towards people who go clubbing, reporting effects they attributed to nitrous oxide, mostly while also using other drugs. The source may be cited for what GDS 2014 respondents reported, with denominators: prevalence in this sample by country, patterns of use among last-year respondents, and the shares reporting each self-attributed effect (about 4630 answering). It may not be cited for population prevalence, for clinically confirmed nerve damage, for a dose–response relation, for dependence, or for claims that use is safe or harmful in general.

key_findings.finding: Prevalence in the whole GDS 2014 sample (n=74,864): lifetime 18.8% (95% CI 18.5–19.1), last 12 months 6.5% (6.3–6.7), last 30 days 2.2% (2.1–2.3); median 2 days of use (IQR 1–3) in the last 30 days.

Among UK respondents nitrous oxide was the eighth most used substance, after alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, ecstasy, caffeinated energy drinks, cocaine and electronic cigarettes; it is not in the worldwide top ten.
key_findings.note: The figure does not say whether the ranking is by lifetime or recent use.

key_findings.finding: Last-year respondents (n=4883): mean age 24.3 (SD 6.7), median 22 (IQR 20–27); last-year prevalence 7.2% among men and 4.9% among women, 9.4% among clubbers and 3.0% among non-clubbers; 89.2% (4354) used nitrous oxide with other drugs.

Places ever used (last-year respondents): private house parties 72.2% (3525), festivals 53.3% (2601), own home 51.4% (2511), clubs 31.8% (1554), work 2.6% (126), other 9.9%; ever bought from friends 38.8% (1892), supermarkets 34.4% (1680), the internet 29.3% (1431), festivals 28.7% (1400), head shops 9.9%, dealers 7.3%, adult stores 6.1%.

Adverse effects experienced in relation to nitrous oxide among last-year respondents (in the last 12 months / earlier only / never): hallucinations 27.8% (1289) / 8.5% (392) / 63.7% (2953); confusion 24.0% (1108) / 7.5% (349) / 68.5% (3165); nausea 5.8% (267) / 3.9% (183) / 90.3% (4180); fainting 4.4% (205) / 6.0% (278) / 89.6% (4170); persistent numbness or tingling 4.3% (200) / 1.6% (74) / 94.1% (4359); accidental injury 1.2% (56) / 2.0% (91) / 96.8% (4498).
key_findings.note: Denominators are not printed; by the editors' sums of each row they are 4622 (confusion) to 4653 (fainting) of the 4883 last-year respondents. Ever reported (editors' calculation): hallucinations 36.3%, confusion 31.5%, fainting 10.4%, nausea 9.7%, persistent numbness 5.9% (274 of 4633), accidents 3.2% (147 of 4645).

key_findings.finding: By sex, in the last 12 months: nausea 8.7% of women (100) and 4.8% of men (162); persistent numbness 4.8% (56) and 4.2% (142); accidents 1.5% (17) and 1.1% (36); hallucinations 24.9% (289) and 28.5% (968). No tests are reported.

Typical amount per session (median hits, IQR) among those reporting each effect in the last 12 months against those who never did: accidents 15 (6–40) vs 5 (3–10); fainting 10 (5–24) vs 5 (3–10); nausea 7 (4–15) vs 5 (3–10); confusion 6 (3–10) vs 4 (2–9); hallucinations 6 (4–12) vs 4 (2–8); persistent numbness 6 (4–12) vs 5 (3–10).
key_findings.locator: Table 3, rows of median hits per session

key_findings.finding: Mean hits per session (95% CI, Poisson) among those reporting each effect: accidents 27.4 (26.0–28.8), fainting 21.1 (20.5–21.7), persistent numbness 15.1 (14.6–15.7), nausea 14.4 (13.9–14.8), hallucinations 12.8 (12.6–13.0); confusion and respondents without effects are not shown. The authors read this ordering as suggesting a dose–response relationship.
key_findings.note: The intervals equal Poisson intervals computed with the number reporting each effect in the last 12 months (for example accidents, n=56: 27.4 ± 1.96 × √(27.4/56), editors' calculation); given the skewed distributions in Table 3 they are far too narrow.

key_findings.finding: Worry among last-year respondents: about effects on mental health, no 77.5% (3611), a little 19.2% (894), a lot 3.3% (152); about effects on physical health, no 76.5% (3568), a little 20.2% (944), a lot 3.3% (152).

Limits stated by the authors: a self-nominating sample that may not represent people who use nitrous oxide; UK respondents were 9% of the sample but 20% of them had used nitrous oxide in the last 12 months, so the findings may reflect the UK drug scene more than a global pattern; retrospective self-report, high levels of other drug use, confounding by other substances and recall bias.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Sampling strategy (PDF p. 3); Limitations (single paragraph, PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Deaths cited as background, not data from this survey: a Virginia review of coroner reports found 2 of 39 accidental inhalant deaths over 10 years directly related to nitrous oxide; the UK Volatile Substance Abuse Mortality Project attributed 5 deaths in 2009 and 52 over 1971–2009 to non-medical nitrous oxide use, the 2009 deaths by asphyxiation with a plastic bag over the head; a 2013 UK death widely reported as due to nitrous oxide followed inhalation of a mislabelled gas.
key_findings.note: The paper prints the Virginia figure as 8% (n=2) of 39 deaths; 2 of 39 is 5% (editors' calculation). Background figures are second-hand and should be cited from their own sources.

key_findings.finding: The paper ends with a box of harm-reduction tips produced by the Global Drug Survey for clinicians (Figure 2). They are the authors' advice, not results of the survey, and are not reproduced on this card.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions, last sentence (PDF p. 5); Figure 2 (PDF p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Median days of use in the last 30 days by effect group (last 12 months against never): accidents 2 (IQR 0–4) against 0 (0–1); fainting 1 (0–2) against 0 (0–1); hallucinations 1 (0–2) against 0 (0–1); persistent numbness 0 (0–2) against 0 (0–1); no test is reported.

The Discussion suggests, hedged, that persistent numbness, given nitrous oxide's effect on vitamin B12 metabolism, may represent heavy or dependent users experiencing neuropathy; it is the paper's only link from the self-reported numbness item to nerve damage.

The authors argue that reasonable general-population inferences can be drawn from large, demographically varied purposive samples, and that their group has previously shown self-report among early-adopting drug-using groups to be valid.

reporting_issues.issue: The bullet-point summary says last-year prevalence was up to 38%; in Table 1, 38.6% is lifetime prevalence among UK respondents, whose last-year prevalence was 20.5%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary roughly doubles the highest last-year figure; Table 1 should be quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Conclusions say use was mainly at festivals and in clubs, but Table 2 shows private house parties (72.2%) and the respondent's own home (51.4%) as common as or more common than festivals (53.3%), with clubs at 31.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Settings of use should be taken from Table 2, not from the abstract.

reporting_issues.issue: Confusion is 23.9% in the abstract and Discussion but 24.0% (1108) in Table 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; 1108 of 4622 is 23.97% (editors' calculation), so Table 3 is right to one decimal.

reporting_issues.issue: The percentages in the abstract are described as shares of last-year respondents (n=4883), but their denominators are the respondents who answered each item (by the editors' sums of Table 3, 4622 to 4653), and they count only experiences in the last 12 months.
reporting_issues.consequence: Quoted shares should state both the denominator and the 12-month window; including earlier experiences, persistent numbness was reported by 5.9% and accidents by 3.2%.

reporting_issues.issue: The intervals in Table 4 are Poisson intervals using the number reporting each effect in the last 12 months (editors' check: accidents, n=56, 26.0–28.8), while Table 3 shows strongly skewed amounts (accidents median 15, IQR 6–40, against a mean of 27.4). Table 4 omits confusion and gives no values for respondents without each effect.
reporting_issues.consequence: The intervals understate uncertainty and the table cannot show a dose–response relation; the medians in Table 3 are the better summary.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says heavy use was associated with persistent numbness, but the median hits per session were 6 (IQR 4–12) among those reporting it in the last 12 months against 5 (3–10) among those who never had it; only the Poisson mean in Table 4 (15.1, with no comparison value) suggests a larger difference.
reporting_issues.consequence: The survey does not support a clear link between amount per session and persistent numbness.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results refer to seven countries, but Table 1 shows six countries and the whole sample.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; country choice is not explained.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 lists a well-being mean score (54.9) without naming the instrument or its range.

The Methods say almost 80,000 people took part, but 74,864 are analysed, with no account of exclusions; the Limitations give the UK as 9% of the sample where Table 1 implies 9.6% (7174 of 74,864, editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; data cleaning is not described.

design_detail: Systematic review of published case reports with pooled patient-level data; the authors call it an individual patient data meta-analysis and cite the MOOSE statement; no protocol or registration is reported. MEDLINE via PubMed, January 1966 to August 2018, with a search string requiring both a nitrous oxide term (including laughing gas and whippets) and a vitamin B12, cobalamin, homocysteine, methylmalonic acid, methionine or folic acid term, plus references of retrieved articles; English only. Case reports were included if they described at least one health outcome after nitrous oxide exposure and gave at least one laboratory value (haemoglobin, haematocrit, MCV, serum folate, homocysteine or methylmalonic acid) before vitamin B12 treatment; cases given B12 before exposure were excluded. 85 publications describing 100 patients were pooled as one sample: proportions with 95% intervals for clinical, laboratory and spinal MRI findings and for the diagnoses reported, a logistic regression of single against regular exposure screening 63 variables, exploratory analyses of exposure amount against outcomes (28 patients), and a principal component analysis described as a check for population stratification. The case reports were not appraised. AMSTAR 2 is applied by analogy, as for earlier pooled case-report reviews on the project.
can_establish: What the 100 published, English-language, laboratory-documented cases of harm after nitrous oxide exposure found in PubMed up to August 2018 looked like: their settings and reported exposure, neurological and haematological findings, B12-related laboratory markers, spinal MRI findings and the diagnoses applied, and how single-exposure (mostly surgical) cases differed from regular-exposure cases.
cannot_establish: How often nitrous oxide harms people who use it recreationally or receive it in medicine (no denominator of exposed people, as the authors concede); whether larger exposure raises the risk (no association found in 28 cases, and published cases are not a sample of exposure); how common B12-related damage is relative to other harms (the search required B12-related terms and the inclusion criteria laboratory values); or a global burden in the usual sense (no incidence, prevalence or population estimate).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: published case reports retrieved from PubMed (492 records) and reference lists (21) (p. 2; Figure 1, p. 5).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: case reports describing at least one health outcome in relation to previous nitrous oxide exposure. Excluded: non-English publications, editorials, narrative reviews, congress abstracts, absence of nitrous oxide exposure, B12 given before exposure, and no value of haemoglobin, haematocrit, MCV, serum folate, homocysteine or methylmalonic acid before B12 treatment (p. 2, 2.2).
sample.demographics: 60 men and 40 women; median age 27 years (IQR 22–36; range 0.4–76.0). Reports came from North America (51), Western Europe (22), China or Taiwan (12) and Australia or New Zealand (10) (pp. 4–5).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Many items were unreported for many patients: haemoglobin reported for 43, haematocrit 21, MCV 55, B12 82, homocysteine 31, methylmalonic acid 16, spinal MRI 75, exposure amount 28 (Tables 1, 2 and 4).
sample.selection_effects: Publication-selected cases: case reports describe unusual, severe or instructive cases, and the review further required a B12-related search term and laboratory values, which selects cases investigated for B12 deficiency. One database, English only. The authors call the compiled cases unselected (p. 14), which the editors do not accept.

exposure.measurement: As reported in each case report: setting (recreational, surgery, occupational, pain management, other), frequency (regular, defined as repeated exposure with at least one cartridge a month, or once), and where available cartridges per day and duration (p. 3, 2.4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Inhalation. Among patients with regular exposure, as reported: median 25 cartridges a day (IQR 8–85; reported for 30), median duration 0.7 years (0.3–1.5; 52), median 18.5 cartridge-years (1.4–99.9; 28), which the authors convert at 8 g a cartridge to 54,020 g (Table 1, p. 6; p. 5). The single exposures were mostly anaesthetic, in the authors' description (p. 13).
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported: none of the described domains of the extraction form (1–5, 7, 9 and 10; domains 6 and 8 are not described) covers other drugs or alcohol, and no such data are reported (p. 3).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Laboratory values had to precede B12 treatment; their timing relative to the last exposure is not reported.

comparison.controls: None. Internal comparison of the 24 single-exposure cases with the 76 regular-exposure cases (Table 5).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: B12 status before exposure, diet, malabsorption or pernicious anaemia, alcohol and other drug use, and genetic variants of one-carbon metabolism are not among the described extraction domains and are not reported (one MTHFR deficiency appears among the diagnoses). The authors' advice to screen B12 before anaesthesia in high-risk groups (p. 14) implies that pre-existing deficiency matters, but it was not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Data extracted from the case reports on a predefined form: clinical findings as binary items (Table 3 lists 45), seven laboratory values (haemoglobin, haematocrit, MCV, B12, folate, homocysteine, methylmalonic acid), the combined indicator of B12 status (cB12, after Fedosov et al.) from B12, homocysteine and methylmalonic acid, the diagnoses reported, setting, exposure, and T2 hyperintensity of the spinal cord on MRI (p. 3, 2.3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Thresholds: WHO definitions for low haemoglobin (below 13.0 g/dL in men, 12.0 g/dL in non-pregnant women) and low haematocrit (below 39% and 36%); B12 below 150 pmol/L; homocysteine above 15 µmol/L; methylmalonic acid above 0.4 µmol/L; folate below 7 µg/L; cB12 categories after Fedosov et al. (pp. 8–9). Assays and reference ranges differ across the case reports and were not harmonized; the diagnoses are those applied by the case authors.
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is whatever the case report described; each percentage is the share of the 100 patients, or of those for whom the item was reported.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 63 variables screened by univariate logistic regression against single exposure, followed by stepwise multivariable selection; exploratory analyses of exposure amount against outcomes are in Table S4 (not read).

analysis.effect_sizes: Proportions with 95% intervals: recreational setting 57.0% (47.1–66.9); regular exposure 76.0% (67.5–84.5); at least one neurological symptom 96% (92.1–99.9); paresthesia, numbness or tingling 80.0% (72.0–88.0); unsteady gait 58.0% (48.2–67.8); weakness 43.0% (33.1–52.9); subacute combined degeneration 28.0% (19.0–37.0); myelopathy 26.0% (17.3–34.7); generalized demyelinating polyneuropathy 23.0% (14.6–31.4); spinal T2 hyperintensity 51 of 75, 68.0% (57.2–78.8); B12 below 150 pmol/L 58 of 82, 70.7% (60.7–80.8); homocysteine above 15 µmol/L 28 of 31, 90.3% (79.3–100); methylmalonic acid above 0.4 µmol/L 15 of 16, 93.8% (80.4–100); cB12 possibly or probably deficient 28 of 33 (84.8%). Single exposure (n=24) against regular: age 40 or older, multivariable OR 23.95 (3.62–158.61); B12 74 pmol/L or lower, 10.57 (1.70–65.90); model AUROC 0.908 (0.795–0.970). Editors' calculation: the printed intervals are reproduced by a Wald interval using the t distribution and n−1, truncated at 0 and 100 (for example 5 of 20 gives 4.2–45.8); Wilson intervals would be, for example, 75.1% to 96.7% for 28 of 31 and 71.7% to 98.9% for 15 of 16.
analysis.covariates: Multivariable model: age 40 or older and B12 74 pmol/L or lower retained by stepwise selection (entry at p<0.1, retention at p<0.05); MCV above 100 fL not retained (p. 4; Table 5).
analysis.selective_reporting: Supplementary Tables S1–S4 and Figures S1–S2 hold the excluded and included studies, the univariate results, the exposure-amount analyses and the stratification plots (not read). The denominator for the share with at least one haematological abnormality is not given. Results for the 60 variables not associated with single exposure are only in Table S3.
analysis.power: Not addressed formally; the authors say missing laboratory data reduced power (p. 14). The multivariable odds ratios rest on 24 single-exposure cases with incomplete B12 data and have wide intervals (age 3.62–158.61; B12 1.70–65.90).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 100 published cases (85 reports, 1966–2018, English, PubMed only, retrieved with B12-related search terms and required laboratory values), most patients were young and had used nitrous oxide recreationally (57) or received it during surgery (25). 96 had at least one neurological symptom, most often paresthesia (80); subacute combined degeneration, myelopathy and demyelinating polyneuropathy were the commonest diagnoses; 51 of 75 with spinal MRI had T2 cord hyperintensity; B12 was below 150 pmol/L in 58 of 82, homocysteine raised in 28 of 31 and methylmalonic acid in 15 of 16. Single-exposure (mostly surgical) cases were older and had lower B12 than regular-exposure cases. Exposure amount, known for 28, was not associated with any finding.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title and abstract present a global burden and the prevalence of findings, but the review counts features among published cases and cannot estimate how often exposure causes harm, as the authors concede in their limitations (p. 15). The abstract's finding of neurological or haematological disorders in almost all published cases (p. 1) largely follows from the selection: inclusion required a reported health outcome and a value for at least one of six laboratory tests (not an abnormal one), and the search required B12-related terms, which together make such findings very likely and partly explain why the burden appears dominated by B12 deficiency (p. 2). The Results' statement that patients had a high risk of macrocytic anaemia (p. 8) rests on a median MCV of 100 fL in the 55 cases with a value, 23 of whom (41.8%) were above 100 fL (Table 4, p. 9); pooled case reports cannot give a risk. The Discussion's claim of a particularly unfavourable risk-benefit ratio for people using nitrous oxide recreationally (p. 12) rests on no assessment of benefit or risk; the more severe clinical picture it attributes to single exposures (p. 13) is not shown in the results; and its description of the compiled case reports as unselected patients (p. 14) misreads publication selection. The recommendations on B12 screening before anaesthesia rest on the ENIGMA trial cited in the Discussion, not on this review's data (pp. 13–14). A headline version (nitrous oxide damages the nerves of 96% of people; most harm is B12 deficiency) would turn a description of published cases into a risk estimate.

timeline.event: Lassen et al.: severe bone-marrow depression after prolonged nitrous oxide anaesthesia in patients treated for tetanus, the first description cited by this review (p. 2); not read for this card.

Imberger et al. (2014), Br J Anaesth: meta-analysis of randomized trials finding no robust evidence on how nitrous oxide in general anaesthesia affects mortality and cardiovascular complications, as described here (p. 14); not read for this card.

Garakani et al. (2016): systematic review of the case literature, without pooled estimates, as described here (p. 14); on the project's Nitrous-oxide reading list (Tier A, item 1); not read for this card.

Kaar et al., Global Drug Survey 2014: among respondents who had used nitrous oxide, 4.3% reported persistent numbness and 1.2% accidental injury, as cited by this review (p. 13); not read for this card.

Winstock and Ferris (2019), J Psychopharmacol: peripheral neuropathy related to the amount of recreational nitrous oxide use; on the project's Nitrous-oxide reading list (Tier A, item 5); not read for this card.

Ménétrier et al. (2023), Antioxidants: systematic review of vitamin B12 status and laboratory abnormalities in people using nitrous oxide recreationally; on the project's Nitrous-oxide reading list (Tier A, item 22); not read for this card.
Brunt et al. (2024), Addiction: review of nitrous oxide and peripheral neurotoxicity; on the project's Nitrous-oxide reading list (Tier A, item 9); not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: only this review was read for this card. It is a quantitative summary of the published case literature up to 2018 and is often quoted for its percentages, which describe published, laboratory-documented cases, not people who use nitrous oxide. The project's Nitrous-oxide reading list places the population survey on neuropathy by amount of use (Winstock and Ferris 2019), later case series and poison-centre data, and the B12-status review (Ménétrier 2023) as the sources for how often, and at what exposure, harm occurs.

funding.funder: Institutional funding from i-Site Lorraine University of Excellence (ANR-15-IDEX-04-LUE), FHU ARRIMAGE and INSERM UMR_S_1256 (p. 15).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest (p. 15).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Lorraine (INSERM unit on nutrition, genetics and environmental risk exposure), University Hospital of Nancy (molecular medicine and biochemistry; reference centre for inborn errors of metabolism) and the University of California, Davis (Green). The authors work on vitamin B12 and one-carbon metabolism: 16 of the 48 references are co-authored by the senior author or by Green (editors' count), including the cB12 method used (reference 9). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts of people who use nitrous oxide recreationally, with recorded exposure, B12, homocysteine and methylmalonic acid measured before and during use, and standardized neurological examination, to give incidence and the relation to amount; a registry of all clinical presentations, not only published ones, to show the spectrum of harms; and, for anaesthesia, trial data that record pre-operative B12 status.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: People with a health outcome after nitrous oxide exposure in medical or recreational settings, the exposure, and the outcomes (clinical, laboratory and MRI findings, diagnoses) are stated; no comparator by design.

domains.domain: 2. Protocol registered before the review (critical)
domains.note: No protocol or registration is reported; the MOOSE statement is cited.

domains.domain: 3. Explanation of study designs included
domains.note: Case reports were chosen because the effects of nitrous oxide are mainly reported through case reports and individual data were wanted (Introduction, p. 2); why case series with group data, cohorts and trials were left out is not explained.

domains.domain: 4. Comprehensive literature search (critical)
domains.note: One database (MEDLINE via PubMed) and reference lists, with the full string given; English only, justified only afterwards by a study of language bias in trial meta-analyses (p. 14); no grey literature or registries. The string also required a B12-related term, so reports not mentioning B12, homocysteine, methylmalonic acid, methionine or folate were not retrieved.

domains.domain: 5. Study selection in duplicate
domains.note: Three investigators reviewed titles and abstracts; whether independently, and how disagreements were settled, is not reported.

domains.domain: 6. Data extraction in duplicate
domains.note: Eight investigators reviewed the eligible articles with a predefined form, and disagreement in data extraction was resolved by consensus, which implies at least two extractors per article (p. 3); the number per article is not stated.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: the excluded full-text studies are in Table S1, which was not read; the text and Figure 1 give 47 exclusions, while the list of supplementary materials calls Table S1 the detail of twenty-nine excluded studies, so the list may be incomplete.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: the included reports are described in Table S2, which was not read; the main text gives only regions of origin and pooled patient characteristics.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No appraisal of the quality or completeness of the case reports with any tool; the principal component analysis looks for population stratification, not for bias in the included reports.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported in the main text.

domains.domain: 11. Appropriate statistical methods for meta-analysis (critical)
domains.note: 100 patients from 85 publications pooled as one sample, with Wald-type intervals truncated at 0 and 100, no allowance for several patients from one report, denominators that change with what each report gave, and a stepwise logistic regression on 63 screened variables with 24 single-exposure cases and missing data.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Not assessed.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The limitations mention missing data, the language restriction and the inability to estimate frequency (pp. 14–15), but the title, abstract and Conclusions present a global burden, and the Discussion calls the compiled cases unselected (p. 14).

domains.domain: 14. Heterogeneity explained and discussed
domains.note: The pooled proportions mix single anaesthetic exposures and months of recreational use without stratifying the main findings; the single-versus-regular comparison examines predictors of exposure type, not how this mixing affects the pooled results.

domains.domain: 15. Publication bias investigated (critical)
domains.note: Not investigated, although which cases get published is the main selection problem in a review of case reports; formal small-study tests do not apply, but the selection is not discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Institutional funding and the authors' declaration of no conflict are reported (p. 15).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: items 7 and 8 can be judged only from supplementary tables that were not read, but the overall rating does not depend on them, because six critical items (2, 4, 9, 11, 13 and 15) are not met, which gives critically low confidence. AMSTAR 2 was built for reviews of intervention studies and is applied here by analogy, as for the project's earlier pooled case-report reviews (sc_strommer_2020, sc_bartolo_2023). The review is a transparent compilation of published cases with stated laboratory definitions, and its counts are internally consistent apart from a few slips. Citable for: what 100 published, English-language, laboratory-documented cases found in PubMed up to August 2018 showed (settings; neurological symptoms in 96; myelopathy and neuropathy diagnoses; spinal T2 lesions in 51 of 75; B12 below 150 pmol/L in 58 of 82; raised homocysteine in 28 of 31 and methylmalonic acid in 15 of 16), and for the older age and lower B12 of single-exposure, mostly surgical cases. Not citable for: how often nitrous oxide harms people who use it, a global burden, dose–response, or the share of all harms that are B12-related.

key_findings.finding: Search: MEDLINE via PubMed, January 1966 to August 2018, with a string requiring a nitrous oxide term (including laughing gas and whippets) and a vitamin B12, cobalamin, homocysteine, methylmalonic acid, methionine or folic acid term, plus references of retrieved articles. Case reports were retained if they described at least one health outcome after nitrous oxide exposure; excluded were non-English publications, editorials, narrative reviews, congress abstracts, cases without exposure, cases given B12 before exposure, and cases without a value of haemoglobin, haematocrit, MCV, serum folate, homocysteine or methylmalonic acid before B12 treatment.
key_findings.locator: 2.1 Data Sources and Searches; 2.2 Study Selection (one paragraph each)

key_findings.finding: 513 records (492 from PubMed and 21 from reference lists) were screened, 381 excluded on title and abstract, 132 assessed in full text and 47 excluded, leaving 85 publications with individual data on 100 patients; reports came mostly from North America (51), Western Europe (22), China or Taiwan (12) and Australia or New Zealand (10).
key_findings.note: Figure 1 is an image; its counts were read on the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: Patients: 60 men and 40 women, median age 27 years (IQR 22–36; range 0.4–76.0). Setting: recreational 57 (57.0%, 95% CI 47.1–66.9), surgery 25 (16.4–33.6), occupational 9, pain management 6, and one each for manipulation under general anaesthesia, Munchausen syndrome and management of sleep disturbance. Regular exposure 76 (67.5–84.5), once 24; of the 76 with regular exposure, 56 were recreational (73.7%), 9 occupational (11.8%) and 6 pain management (7.9%).

Among patients with regular exposure: median 25 cartridges a day (IQR 8–85; reported for 30), median duration 0.7 years (0.3–1.5; reported for 52) and median 18.5 cartridge-years (1.4–99.9; reported for 28), which the authors equate with 54,020 g of nitrous oxide at 8 g a cartridge.
key_findings.locator: 2.4 Nitrous Oxide Exposure (p. 3); 3.2, 2nd paragraph (p. 5); Table 1, quantitative estimates (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Reported diagnoses (of 100; more than one possible): subacute combined degeneration 28 (95% CI 19.0–37.0), myelopathy 26 (17.3–34.7), generalized demyelinating polyneuropathy 23 (14.6–31.4), vitamin B12 deficiency 14, axonal polyneuropathy 11, encephalopathy 2, toxicity with no specific diagnosis 19. Spinal cord T2 hyperintensity in 51 of the 75 with MRI (68.0%, 57.2–78.8).

At least one neurological symptom in 96% (92.1–99.9): paresthesia, numbness or tingling 80 (72.0–88.0), unsteady gait or walking difficulty 58 (48.2–67.8), weakness 43 (33.1–52.9), falls or equilibrium disorders 24, Lhermitte's sign 15, ataxia 12, cognitive decline 9, urinary incontinence 8, quadriparesis or paralysis 7, behaviour alteration 6, impaired memory 5, depression 4, thrombo-occlusive event 3, paranoid behaviour 3, visual hallucination 2, suicidal thought 1 (of 100).

Haematology: median MCV 100 fL (IQR 94–103; n=55); median haemoglobin 12.8 g/dL in men (10.8–14.2; n=23) and 10.7 g/dL in women (8.3–12.4; n=20); low haemoglobin by WHO thresholds in 24 of 43 (55.8%), low haematocrit in 52.4% of 21, MCV above 100 fL in 23 of 55 (41.8%); at least one haematological abnormality in 71.7% (59.9–83.4), denominator not stated.
key_findings.note: Two reporting slips affect this finding (low haematocrit count; missing denominator); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: B12-related markers: median B12 101 pmol/L (IQR 74–161; n=82), below 150 pmol/L in 58 of 82 (70.7%, 60.7–80.8); median homocysteine 55 µmol/L (29–111), above 15 µmol/L in 28 of 31 (90.3%, 79.3–100); median methylmalonic acid 5.0 µmol/L (1.1–6.6), above 0.4 µmol/L in 15 of 16 (93.8%, 80.4–100); median serum folate 12.8 µg/L (7.3–14.6), below 7 µg/L in 5 of 20 (25.0%). cB12 (n=33): probably deficient 19 (57.6%), possibly deficient 9 (27.3%), decreased 2 (6.1%), adequate 3 (9.1%), elevated 0; possibly or probably deficient 84.8%.

Single exposure against regular exposure: medians age 47 against 26 years, B12 74 against 110 pmol/L, MCV 104 against 97 fL; of 63 variables screened, three were associated with single exposure in univariate analysis (age 40 or older OR 23.33, 6.84–79.61; B12 74 pmol/L or lower 6.06, 2.05–17.90; MCV above 100 fL 9.75, 1.93–49.15), and two remained in the multivariable model (age 40 or older OR 23.95, 3.62–158.61, p=0.001; B12 74 pmol/L or lower 10.57, 1.70–65.90, p=0.01), with AUROC 0.908 (0.795–0.970).

Exposure amount was available for 28 patients; in exploratory analyses it was not significantly correlated with any biological variable, nor associated with the commonest diagnoses, the commonest clinical findings or spinal T2 hyperintensity.
key_findings.locator: 3.3.2 Association Between the Amount of Nitrous Oxide Exposure and Outcomes (one paragraph)
key_findings.note: Detailed results are in Table S4, not read; with 28 published cases, absence of an association says little.

key_findings.finding: Bias was assessed only as population stratification, by visual inspection of principal-component plots of the patients' variables, which showed no significant stratification (Figure S1); the case reports were not appraised and publication selection was not examined.
key_findings.locator: 2.7 Assessment of Bias (p. 4); 3.3.3 Assessment of Bias (p. 12)

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: data from available case reports risk missing data; laboratory findings were not available for all patients, reducing power; thromboembolic events after surgery may have been attributed to the operation rather than to nitrous oxide; non-English reports were excluded; and because the review rests on single reports or small series it cannot evaluate how often nitrous oxide toxicity occurs, which may be rare given how widely the gas is used.

Figures the Discussion cites from other sources: in the 2016/17 Crime Survey for England and Wales, 2.6% of adults aged 16–59 (around 840,000) and 9.3% of 16–24-year-olds had used nitrous oxide in the preceding year; in the Global Drug Survey 2014 (74,864 participants in 17 countries), lifetime use was reported by 38.6% of respondents in the UK and 29.4% in the US, and among respondents who had used nitrous oxide, persistent numbness was reported by 4.3% and accidental injury by 1.2%; in the Global Drug Survey 2016 (over 100,000 respondents from over 50 countries), 4% of respondents who had used nitrous oxide reported symptoms of nerve damage.
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures, not this review's data; the 2014 survey analysis is Kaar et al. (2016).

key_findings.finding: The Discussion's advice on B12 assessment before nitrous oxide anaesthesia rests on the ENIGMA trial it cites, in surgical patients: 215 given nitrous oxide-containing and 179 nitrous oxide-free anaesthesia, with postoperative hyperhomocysteinaemia OR 3.91 (1.82–8.40) for nitrous oxide, and OR 0.09 (0.03–0.28) in patients given B vitamins before surgery. The review's Conclusions leave it to future population studies to test whether correcting B12 deficiency prevents nitrous oxide toxicity.
key_findings.note: Second-hand trial data (Myles et al., 2008), not this review's data.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 4, low haematocrit status is printed as n = 21 of N = 21 with 52.4% (29.1–75.7). Editors' calculation: 52.4% of 21 is 11, and 11 of 21 reproduces both the percentage and the printed interval.
Figure 1 and the text give 47 full-text exclusions listed in Table S1, while the list of supplementary materials describes Table S1 as the detail of twenty-nine excluded studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: The list of excluded studies may be incomplete; AMSTAR 2 item 7 cannot be settled without the supplement.

reporting_issues.issue: At least one haematological abnormality is reported in 71.7% (59.9–83.4%), in the abstract and the Results, without a denominator; the haemoglobin, haematocrit and MCV items were reported for 43, 21 and 55 patients. Editors' calculation: 43 of 60 reproduces the percentage and interval.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure cannot be checked from the paper; cite it with its uncertain denominator or use the item-level counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say principal components were computed from the ten top eigenvalues; the Results describe plots based on the top five.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the analysis is in any case not an assessment of risk of bias in the included reports.

reporting_issues.issue: The extraction form is said to have 10 domains, but only domains 1 to 5, 7, 9 and 10 are described; and the probably-deficient cB12 category is defined in the Methods as cB12 < 2.5, but in Table 4 as < −2.5.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; Table 4's definition (below −2.5) is the one that fits the other categories.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Figure 3 repeats the text of Figure 2's legend (proportions of clinical, laboratory and radiological findings, and the WHO haemoglobin and haematocrit thresholds), which does not describe Figure 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typesetting error; Figure 3 shows the cB12 categories, whose values are in Table 4.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 5 has a column headed AUROC, p-Value that gives only p-values (0.0076, 0.0002 and <0.0001); the areas under the curve for age, B12 and MCV are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: How well each cut-off separates single from regular exposure cannot be judged.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says three-quarters of patients had a low B12 status (below 150 pmol/L) and that neurological or haematological disorders were seen in 96%; Table 4 gives 58 of the 82 patients with a B12 value (70.7%), and 96% is the share with at least one neurological symptom.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the table figures: 58 of 82 with B12 below 150 pmol/L; 96 of 100 with at least one neurological symptom.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 2.5 names predictors of regular exposure as a secondary outcome, and the list of supplementary materials titles Table S3 as variables associated with regular exposure, whereas the analysis plan (2.6), section 3.3.1 and Table 5 model short (single) exposure, the inverse.
reporting_issues.consequence: The odds ratios reported are for a single exposure, as Table 5 labels them (for example age 40 or older, OR 23.95); Table S3 (not read) may be labelled the other way.

Text extracted with pdftotext (pp. 5, 8 and 10 carry a hidden duplicate text layer from the peer-review version; the visible pages were used); pages 1–15 checked on 130-dpi renders, with 300-dpi renders of Table 4 and Table 5. Supplementary Tables S1–S4 and Figures S1–S2 (online at the publisher, no separate DOI) were not among the files and were not read.

disagreements.first_pass: Figures the Discussion cites from other sources: in the 2016/17 Crime Survey for England and Wales, 2.6% of adults aged 16–59 (around 840,000) and 9.3% of 16–24-year-olds had used nitrous oxide in the preceding year; in the Global Drug Survey 2014 (74,864 participants), lifetime use was 38.6% in the UK and 29.4% in the US, and among those who had used it, persistent numbness was reported by 4.3% and accidental injury by 1.2%; the 2016 survey found 4% with symptoms of nerve damage.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 543 (round-2 check): corrected; the Global Drug Survey 2014 covered 17 countries, and the 2016 survey (over 100,000 respondents from over 50 countries) found that 4% of those who had used nitrous oxide had symptoms of nerve damage (pp. 13–14).
disagreements.resolution: Accepted with changes (pp. 13–14, 4. Discussion, 6th paragraph): 17 countries and the 2016 survey's size are added, and the 4% is now tied to respondents who had used nitrous oxide, not to all respondents; as survey findings, the lifetime-use shares and the 4% are written as respondents' reports.

disagreements.first_pass: The abstract's finding of neurological or haematological disorders in almost all published cases (p. 1) is built into the inclusion criteria (a reported health outcome and laboratory values), and the burden being dominated by B12 deficiency partly reflects a search that required B12-related terms (p. 2).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 543 (round-2 check): substantial agreed; built into the inclusion criteria is a little strong: inclusion required a reported outcome and any one laboratory value, not an abnormal one; with the B12-term search it makes such findings near-certain.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading p. 2, 2.1 and 2.2: inclusion required at least one health outcome and a value of one of six laboratory tests before B12 treatment, not an abnormal value. The sentence now says the finding largely follows from the selection and the B12-term search. The gap stays substantial.

disagreements.first_pass: Not extracted: the extraction form has no item for other drugs or alcohol (p. 3). Elsewhere: comparison.unmeasured_premorbid, B12 status before exposure, diet, malabsorption or pernicious anaemia, alcohol and other drug use, and genetic variants of one-carbon metabolism were not extracted.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 543 (round-2 check), missed: exposure.polysubstance says the form has no item for other drugs or alcohol; only domains 1-5, 7, 9 and 10 are described (6 and 8 are not), so say none of the described domains, and that no such data are reported.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading p. 3, 2.3: the form is said to have 10 domains, of which eight are described, none on alcohol or other drugs. Both fields now say the described domains do not cover these factors and that no such data are reported.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 543 (round-2 check), missed: Section 2.5 names predictors of regular exposure as a secondary outcome (and Table S3 is titled for regular exposure), while 3.3.1 and Table 5 model short exposure, the inverse (pp. 3, 10-11, 15).
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading p. 3, 2.5; p. 4, 2.6 (short exposure as the dependent variable); p. 10, 3.3.1; p. 11, Table 5; and p. 15, Supplementary Materials (title of Table S3). It bears on the direction of the odds ratios a reader cites, so it is entered as a reporting issue; key_findings[8] already gives them for single exposure.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 543 (round-2 check), missed: the Results say patients had a high risk of macrocytic anemia (p. 8) from case-report medians (MCV 100 fL in 55), a risk statement the case data cannot support.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading p. 8, 3.2, 4th paragraph, and p. 9, Table 4 (median MCV 100 fL, IQR 94–103, n=55; MCV above 100 fL in 23 of 55, 41.8%): pooled case reports cannot give a risk, and fewer than half had an MCV above 100 fL; one sentence added to interpretation_gap.claimed.
